preamble: Unrounding of the rounded vowel /œ/ to [ə], merging it with schwa. Afrikaans has a short rounded /œ/ (krul, bus, brug /brœχ/) whose unrounded counterpart is the central /ə/ of wind and hitte rather than the front /ɛ/ (Wissing 2020); Swanepoel (1927) wrote that both [ɛ] and [ə], "especially the latter", serve as its unrounded equivalent. He already called "the spreading of the rounded vowel" (krul > [krəl], skuld > [skəlt]) the most serious mistake of both English and Afrikaans speakers, warned that the rounded vowel was in grave danger of disappearing from Afrikaans, and listed the word pairs that would then fall together (kul – kil, stuk – stik, sug – sig, rug – rig, put – pit). Wissing (1994), citing Ponelis (1990), notes eighteenth-century spellings such as brig for brug and hilp for hulp; in his experiment one speaker made no durational difference between intended rounded and unrounded front vowels, listeners recognised fewer than half of the intended rounded vowels as rounded, and he reports large-scale derounding in everyday spoken Afrikaans, even in formal radio speech. Wissing (2020) describes the change as age-graded: speakers over 70 deround less than young speakers, only three of twelve students in one test made a clear distinction between /ə/ and /œ/, and in his words the results point in the direction of two chronolects and could also be evidence for a diachronic shift, while absolute neutralization of the contrast has not yet taken place. Derounding is favoured by fast speech and lack of stress but is not limited to them. Because the sources keep /œ/ and /ə/ apart as phonemes and record speakers who still contrast them, this is a merger in progress, not two transcriptions of one vowel. Phonetically Afrikaans /œ/ is a weakly rounded central vowel ([ɞ̝] or [ɞ]); the atlas keeps the symbol œ used by all the sources.

examples.note: Swanepoel (1927: 38–39) gives krul [krœl] as an example of the rounded vowel and [krəl] as its unrounded pronunciation by both Afrikaans and English speakers.
Listed by Swanepoel (1927: 39) among the words in which the rounded vowel is spread (unrounded).
One of Wissing's stimulus words for /œ/ (with uur for /y/ and neus for /ø/); derounding turned its vowel into [ə], more often at a fast speaking rate (Wissing 2020, Vowel derounding).
Wikipedia (after Donaldson 1993): /œns/ is realised as [œns] or [œ̃ːs], which for speakers with the /œ–ə/ merger are [əns] and [ə̃ːs].
